lesson.title: Counting in Twos: The Binary Number System
lesson.summary: Explains how binary (base-2) numbers represent quantities using only 0 and 1, why computers rely on this system, and how to convert between binary and decimal.
lesson.body:
You already know that a computer is a machine built to store and manipulate information, but you may not have thought carefully about what "information" looks like once it's inside the machine. The answer, at the lowest level, is numbers written in base 2 instead of the base 10 you use every day. Understanding why requires stepping back and looking at what a number base actually means.

When you write the decimal number 347, you're using positional notation: each digit's contribution depends on where it sits. The 7 is worth 7, the 4 is worth 4 tens, and the 3 is worth 3 hundreds, because each position represents a power of ten (10^0, 10^1, 10^2). Binary works exactly the same way, except the only digits available are 0 and 1, and each position represents a power of two instead of ten. So the binary number 1011 means, reading right to left, one 1 (2^0), one 2 (2^1), zero 4s (2^2), and one 8 (2^3). Add those up ,  8 + 0 + 2 + 1 ,  and you get 11 in decimal. Every binary number is just a sum of selected powers of two, chosen by which positions hold a 1.

This raises the obvious question: why would a computer bother with a number system that needs four digits to write "11" when decimal does it in two? The answer isn't about arithmetic convenience ,  it's about physical reliability. Inside a computer, information is stored and moved using electronic components that are easiest to build and control when they only need to distinguish between two clearly different states, such as "on" and "off," or a higher voltage versus a lower one. Trying to reliably detect ten distinct voltage levels (to represent decimal digits 0-9) would make circuits far more sensitive to noise and error. Two states are much easier to keep unambiguous, so hardware is built around binary, and every number, letter, image, and instruction a computer handles is ultimately encoded as some sequence of 0s and 1s. Each individual 0 or 1 is called a bit, short for "binary digit."

Converting decimal to binary uses the same place-value logic in reverse. Take the decimal number 13. You can find its binary form by repeatedly dividing by 2 and tracking the remainders: 13 ÷ 2 = 6 remainder 1; 6 ÷ 2 = 3 remainder 0; 3 ÷ 2 = 1 remainder 1; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 remainder 1. Reading the remainders from last to first gives 1101. Check it the way you checked 1011 above: 1101 means one 8, one 4, zero 2s, one 1 ,  that's 8 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 13. It matches, because each division step is really asking "how many of this power of two fit, with what's left over for smaller powers."

As you move forward in this book, you'll see binary underlying almost everything ,  how numbers are stored in variables, how images and text get encoded, and how logical true/false values map naturally onto 1 and 0. The core idea to hold onto is simple: binary isn't a trick or a shortcut, it's the same positional counting system you've always used, just built on powers of two instead of powers of ten, because that's the counting system electronic hardware can represent most reliably.
